title: Labor's 30 per cent minimum tax on family trusts clears parliament
excerpt: A 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trust income has passed parliament after a deal with the Greens. Here's who it affects and when.
content_html:
Discretionary trusts will pay tax of at least 30 per cent on their net income from July 2028, after the federal government's trust tax laws passed parliament this week with the support of the Greens.

What happened

The Senate passed the two trust tax bills on Wednesday night, with six government amendments made to the main bill. The amended bill went back to the House of Representatives on Thursday for final approval, and NCA NewsWire described it as the last piece of legislation from the May budget to pass before parliament rose for the year.

The Greens agreed to back the package in exchange for changes elsewhere. The government will consult in 2027 on raising annual registration fees for private jets, which the Greens argue pay far less in fuel tax than motorists. Emergency, medical, government charter and most business flights, including agricultural use, are intended to be excluded. The deal also includes extra funding for the Australian Taxation Office and the charities regulator, and tighter rules on distributions to tax-exempt bodies where a benefit flows back to the person making them.

How the tax works

From 1 July 2028, the trustee of a discretionary trust must pay at least 30 per cent tax on the trust's net income. Individual beneficiaries then receive a non-refundable credit for the tax already paid, so people on higher personal rates top up the difference while those on lower rates cannot claim the excess back.

Company beneficiaries, often called bucket companies, do not receive the credit. Small business publication SmartCompany reported this means income routed through a company could effectively be taxed twice.

Fixed trusts, superannuation funds, deceased estates, genuine testamentary trusts and income from primary production are outside the new rules, according to a summary by tax adviser PRATT Partners. A government amendment means people with existing wills that set up testamentary trusts should not need to rewrite them.

Why it matters

Discretionary trusts let trustees decide each year how income is shared among family members and other beneficiaries, who may be on lower tax rates. The government says the change makes the system fairer and will help fund tax cuts for workers.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said "more than 90 per cent of small businesses will not be affected" in any year.

Business groups strongly disagree. "Today is a dark day for small businesses," Council of Small Business Organisations Australia chief executive Skye Cappuccio said, according to Accountants Daily. CPA Australia told a Senate hearing that families and businesses could spend $2 billion to $2.8 billion on professional advice to adjust, and COSBOA estimates restructuring a business could cost $15,000 to $50,000 before stamp duty.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor labelled the arrangement with the Greens a dirty deal. The Coalition tried unsuccessfully to split the trust measures from the rest of the bill or delay the start to July 2029, and Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has said a Coalition government would repeal the tax.

What it means for you

  • Trust owners: there are three broad options. Keep the trust and pay the minimum tax, elect into a fixed distribution arrangement that locks in nominated beneficiaries, or restructure into a company or fixed trust.
  • Restructuring: rollover relief is available for three years, from 1 July 2027 to 30 June 2030, to help move assets without triggering some tax costs. Stamp duty is set by the states and may still apply.
  • Everyone else: people without a trust are not directly affected.

The changes are complex, and individual circumstances vary. Trust owners may want to speak with a registered tax agent before acting.

What's next

The laws now need royal assent. The government has said further tax legislation will follow in 2027, and funding details for the tax office and charities regulator will be settled in the 2027-28 budget. Accounting bodies had pushed for a one-year delay, which was not adopted.
